title: An Inspector Calls: the Playwright, Context and Setting
summary: Who J. B. Priestley was, why the play is set in 1912 but was written in 1945, and why the single dining-room setting matters.

p: John Boynton (J. B.) Priestley (1894 to 1984) was a well-known English novelist, playwright and broadcaster. He was a socialist who worried about social inequality and injustice. He believed that the wealthy business class was selfish and that society could improve only if people took collective responsibility for each other. This belief is the foundation of An Inspector Calls.

When the play is set: 1912. This was Edwardian England, shortly before the First World War, a time of strict class division and false confidence. The wealthy factory-owning class (the Birlings) lived in comfort, while the working class (like Eva Smith) had no rights and no safety net. Mr Birling boasts that the Titanic is 'unsinkable', which the audience knows to be tragically wrong.

When it was written: 1945, at the end of the Second World War. Priestley and his audience had lived through two world wars and the Great Depression. They knew that the selfish attitudes of 1912 had helped to lead to disaster. In 1945 Britain was planning a fairer society (the Welfare State).

The purpose: Priestley sets the play in the past to warn the present. He is saying: 'Look at the arrogance of these people. This is what caused our troubles. We must never go back to this. We must be responsible for one another.'

The whole play happens in the dining room of the Birling family's house in the industrial town of Brumley. The room is comfortable and 'prosperous' but 'not cosy'. The single setting is symbolic: the Birlings are trapped in a pressure cooker with the Inspector, and their bubble of wealth is about to burst. Because the action takes place in one room and in real time, the audience feels the same tension and cannot escape, just as the family cannot.

activity: Explain the importance of the play being set in 1912 but written in 1945.

title: An Inspector Calls: Plot
summary: The three acts: the Birling celebration, the Inspector's chain of events, the confessions of Eric and the final telephone call.

p: The Birling family (Arthur, his wife Sybil, daughter Sheila and son Eric) celebrate Sheila's engagement to Gerald Croft, son of a rival business owner. Mr Birling makes a pleased speech about capitalism, saying that 'a man has to mind his own business and look after himself and his own'. Just then the doorbell rings. Inspector Goole arrives, a mysterious and commanding man, to investigate the suicide of a young working-class woman, Eva Smith.

He explains that a 'chain of events' led to her death, and questions the family one by one. Mr Birling sacked Eva from his factory two years earlier because she led a strike for a small rise (from 22 shillings and sixpence to 25 shillings a week). He feels no regret. Eva then found work in a dress shop, Milward's, but Sheila, in a fit of jealousy and bad temper, had her dismissed because she thought the girl had smiled at her. Unlike her father, Sheila is horrified and feels remorse at once.

Sheila suspects that Gerald also knew the girl, and the Inspector proves it. Last summer Gerald met a girl called Daisy Renton (Eva's other name), rescued her from a rude local councillor and set her up in rooms as his mistress. He dropped her when it suited him. Gerald is ashamed but tries to excuse himself.

Mrs Birling, head of a women's charity, refused help to a pregnant young woman who called herself 'Mrs Birling', because she was offended by the girl's 'impertinence'. She told the girl to look for the father of the child and blamed him entirely. She insists that he should be 'made an example of'. The Inspector says, 'Then wait', as Eric Birling walks back into the room. The act ends on this cliffhanger.

img.alt: Five boxes in a row showing how Arthur Birling, Sheila, Gerald, Eric and Sybil Birling each harmed Eva Smith, with an arrow to her death

p: Eric confesses that he is the father. He met Eva ('Daisy') in a bar, got drunk and forced his way into her room. When she became pregnant he panicked and stole money from his father's office to support her. Eva refused to keep the stolen money, which shows that she had better morals than he did.

The Inspector then gives his last speech: 'There are millions and millions and millions of Eva Smiths and John Smiths still left with us... We are members of one body. We are responsible for each other.' He warns that men who do not learn this will be taught 'in fire and blood and anguish'. He leaves.

Afterwards Gerald phones and finds that there is no Inspector Goole on the local police force, and Mr Birling learns that no girl has died today. The older Birlings and Gerald are delighted and think that it was all a hoax. They mock Eric and Sheila. But Sheila and Eric say it does not matter: 'We all did what we did.' They have changed.

The final twist: the phone rings. Mr Birling answers. A girl has just died on her way to the Infirmary after swallowing disinfectant, and an inspector is on his way to ask questions. The family stare in shock, and the play ends.

activity: Summarise Mr Birling's and Sheila's part in the death of Eva Smith, and write a 250-word analysis of how Sheila changes. (Mr Birling sacked Eva for leading a strike; Sheila had her sacked from a shop out of jealousy.)

title: An Inspector Calls: Themes, Style and Characters
summary: Collective responsibility, class hypocrisy, the old and the young, and judgement; the well-made play, dramatic irony and the single setting; and the characters.

p: Social and collective responsibility: the main message, shown in the Inspector's last speech ('We are members of one body'). Priestley argues against the capitalist view of 'every man for himself' and demands that we care for the Eva Smiths of the world.

Class hypocrisy and inequality: the play shows the rotten core under the respectable surface of the Edwardian upper class. The Birlings use the poor (Mr Birling), abuse them (Eric and Gerald) and refuse them charity (Mrs Birling), while believing themselves to be good and moral.

The older against the younger generation: the older Birlings are set in their selfish ways and learn nothing. The younger ones (Sheila and Eric) can feel remorse, change and accept responsibility. They are the hope for the future.
Judgement and time: the Inspector gives a warning, and the family fails it. The telephone call at the end suggests that the real consequences are still to come.
The 'well-made play': a tight three-act structure in which tension grows, secrets are revealed one at a time, and there is a striking climax and a twist ending.
Dramatic irony: the audience knows that Mr Birling is wrong about the Titanic and about the likelihood of war, so his whole philosophy looks foolish from the start.
The single setting: one room makes the play tense and claustrophobic. The Birlings cannot escape the Inspector or their own guilt.

Inspector Goole: the driving force. Mysterious, all-knowing, commanding and single-minded. His name sounds like 'ghoul', which suggests a ghost or an angel: the voice of Priestley's social conscience, sent to judge the family.
Arthur Birling: pompous, selfish and arrogant; he stands for the faults of capitalism.
Sybil Birling: colder and crueller than her husband, a snob obsessed with class and reputation, who feels no remorse.
Sheila Birling: the most changed. She starts as a naive, giggling girl and becomes a strong, perceptive and moral young woman, the play's new conscience.
Eric Birling: weak and nervous, spoilt by his parents' example, but able to feel guilt and to want to change.
Gerald Croft: the 'in-betweener', polished and upper-class, who at last sides with the older generation, putting business and reputation before morality.

The play is a parable. Eva Smith stands for the whole working class, and the Birlings for the ruling class. Priestley's message is a command: if we do not learn to look after each other and share, we shall repeat the cycle of 'fire and blood and anguish' (wars and revolutions).

title: A Man for All Seasons: the Playwright, History and the Central Conflict
summary: Who Robert Bolt was, the history behind the play (Henry VIII's divorce and the Act of Supremacy) and Sir Thomas More's dilemma.

p: Robert Bolt (1924 to 1995) was an English playwright and screenwriter, famous for the films Lawrence of Arabia and Doctor Zhivago. Like Priestley, he held strong political views and was once arrested for protesting against nuclear weapons. But where Priestley wrote about collective responsibility, Bolt was interested in the individual conscience and the conflict between a person's private self and the demands of the state.
The play is based on a real conflict in 16th-century England.
The King's 'Great Matter': King Henry VIII was married to Catherine of Aragon, who had given him a daughter (Mary) but no male heir. Henry wanted a divorce so that he could marry Anne Boleyn.
The religious conflict: England was a Catholic country and the Pope in Rome was head of the Church. The Pope, under pressure from Spain (Catherine's homeland), would not grant the divorce.
The break with Rome: Henry broke with the Catholic Church, made himself 'Supreme Head of the Church of England' and granted himself the divorce.
The Oath of Supremacy: to force his subjects to accept this, Henry made them swear an oath (under the Act of Supremacy) recognising his new title. Refusing the oath was treason, punishable by death.
Sir Thomas More was one of the most respected men in England: a brilliant lawyer, a devout Catholic, Lord Chancellor (the highest office after the King), and a personal friend of Henry VIII.

More is trapped. As an Englishman he wants to obey his King. As a Catholic he cannot accept that the King is head of the Church; his conscience forbids it. As a lawyer, he knows that if he simply stays silent the law cannot convict him of treason, because treason needs an act or a spoken word and not a thought.
So the play is about More's attempt to use silence as a shield to save his life without betraying his conscience. His enemies, such as Thomas Cromwell, must bend the law and use lies to trap him.

title: A Man for All Seasons: Plot, Themes and Characters
summary: The main events of the play, the themes of integrity, conscience, power and the law, and the characters of More, Rich, Cromwell and the Common Man.

p: Richard Rich, an ambitious young man, asks Sir Thomas More for a post at court. More advises him to be a teacher, and refuses to help him get power. Cardinal Wolsey dies and More becomes Lord Chancellor. King Henry visits More at his house and asks for his support for the divorce. More cannot give it, because of his conscience. Rich, meanwhile, turns to Thomas Cromwell, the King's ruthless minister, and starts to rise by betraying More.

More resigns as Chancellor rather than approve the King's plans. Cromwell searches for a way to make him speak. The Act of Supremacy is passed and More refuses the oath. He is sent to the Tower of London. His wife Alice and daughter Margaret beg him to give way, but More will not. At his trial, More says nothing against the King. Rich gives false evidence (perjury) that More denied the King's title. In return, he is made Attorney-General for Wales. More is found guilty. Once he is condemned, he finally speaks openly, saying that the law has been twisted. He is executed in 1535.

Integrity and conscience: the title means that More's 'self' is so firm that he is the same man in every 'season', in good times and in bad. He will not sell his soul. His opposite is Richard Rich, a man for no season, who is bought with power and commits perjury to condemn More.
More's famous line to Rich asks what a man gains by losing his soul for the whole world, 'but for Wales, Richard?'
Power: the state against the individual. The play asks whether a person may refuse the state if the state does wrong.
The law, morality and silence: More loves the law and uses it as a shield. He thinks that silence keeps him safe. His tragedy is that his enemies break the law (with a lying witness) to destroy him.

Sir Thomas More: intelligent, witty, loving, a firm man of conscience. Richard Rich: ambitious, weak and corrupt. Thomas Cromwell: ruthless, practical and willing to bend the law. King Henry VIII: charming but selfish and powerful. Alice and Margaret: More's loving family, who beg him to save himself. The Common Man: a character who plays many small parts (More's steward, a boatman, the jailer, a juror and the executioner). He stands for the average person who is practical, not heroic, and 'goes along' with those in power to survive, the opposite of More's heroic integrity.

activity: Contrast Thomas More and Richard Rich. What does each value? (More values conscience and integrity; Rich values position and power.)
